docs.title: Customer Advocacy in Technical Documentation
docs.text: Customer advocacy is a core principle of my work as a technical writer. I view documentation not as a standalone deliverable, but as a product that must serve multiple audiences with different needs. By actively engaging with customers, developers, product managers, and fellow writers, I ensure that documentation is accurate, usable, and aligned with real-world workflows.

docs.title: External Customers: Clear, Findable, and Usable Documentation
docs.text:
External customers consistently want documentation that is clear, concise, and easy to find and understand. My goal is to reduce the time it takes for customers to get value from a product by presenting information in a straightforward, task-focused way.

I achieve this by applying DITA principles and disciplined writing practices, including clear information architecture, consistent terminology, and reusable content structures. This approach helps ensure that documentation is scannable, logically organized, and easy to maintain over time.

To continuously improve content quality, I actively engage with customer feedback channels, including support tickets, documentation feedback, and pull requests. These inputs help me identify gaps, clarify confusing areas, and add missing context so the documentation evolves alongside customer needs.

docs.title: Internal Customers: Developers and Product Managers
docs.text:
Developers and product managers are also key customers of documentation. My hands-on technical background allows me to work independently, reducing the time required from engineering and product teams while still producing accurate and meaningful content.

By coming prepared and asking specific, targeted questions, I enable these teams to stay focused on their primary responsibilities. I validate assumptions through direct experimentation, code reviews, and testing, and then use focused follow-ups only where clarification is truly needed. This approach builds trust, accelerates delivery, and minimizes disruption to development workflows.

docs.title: Technical Writing Community: Mentorship and Enablement
docs.text:
My third customer group is my fellow technical writers. I support the team by mentoring new and experienced writers, sharing best practices, and helping others navigate tools, processes, and review workflows.

I also create templates, guidelines, and training materials that promote consistency and reduce onboarding time. By documenting processes and establishing repeatable patterns, I help scale the team’s effectiveness while maintaining a high bar for qua

docs.title: Early Design Engagement and Collaboration
docs.text:
Throughout my career, I have workedupstream with product, engineering, and UX teams to influence design decisions before documentation plans were finalized. By partnering early in the development lifecycle, I act as a customer experience advocate, by identifying friction points, shaping workflows, and helping teams avoid downstream rework.

My background as a developer and tester allows me to recognize design and usability issues early, often before they surface as defects or documentation gaps. I approach documentation as product feedback rather than a downstream task, using it to improve clarity, reduce operational overhead, and create more intuitive customer experiences.

docs.title: Approach, Consistency, and Innovation
docs.text:
I regularly participate in design reviews, testing sessions, and working sessions with product managers, engineers, and designers to evaluate workflows, UI text, APIs, and error handling. In these sessions, I focus on clarity, usability (including 508 compliance) and consistency. This provides a customer experience that is aligned across the console UX, documentation, and marketing pages.

I also apply cross-service knowledge to surface recurring patterns and prevent repeated friction, sharing lessons learned across teams to accelerate development and improve integration quality. This perspective is grounded in hands-on development and testing experience, allowing me to anticipate real-world usage and edge cases.

Innovation is a constant throughout my career. I am the inventor on U.S. Patent 7,804,907, “Method and approach for validation and error resolution of configuration data in a private branch exchange switch.” This work reflects a long-standing focus on clear validation, meaningful error messaging, and effective resolution paths—principles I continue to apply when influencing product design, APIs, and documentation today.

This partnering allows me to create documentation that is accurate, cohesive, and customer-focused because it is informed by both design intent and real operational experience.

docs.title: Project Manager
docs.text:
I bring a project management mindset to every initiative, combining customer advocacy, technical depth, and design influence with disciplined execution. My approach is grounded in hands-on experience, strong collaboration practices, and formal Agile training.

I am a Certified ScrumMaster (CSM), which strengthens my ability to manage work in iterative, fast-moving environments while keeping teams aligned and focused on delivering customer value. Certified ScrumMaster – Scrum Alliance

docs.title: Cross-Functional Teamwork
docs.text:
Developers and product managers are also key customers of my work. My hands-on background as a developer and tester allows me to work independently, validate assumptions, and reduce the time required from engineering teams.

I come prepared with context and ask specific, pointed questions, enabling product and engineering partners to stay focused on their primary responsibilities. This approach improves velocity, reduces rework, and supports effective sprint planning and delivery—aligned with Agile and Scrum practices.

As a Certified Scrum Master, I am comfortable working within sprint cycles, managing dependencies, and supporting continuous improvement through retrospectives and feedback loops. I actively work with teams using Jira, Asana, and Monday.com to facilitatle and lead meetings and drive schedules to successful completion.

docs.title: Alignment Across UX, Documentation, and Marketing
docs.text:
Successful projects require a consistent customer experience across all touchpoints. I actively look for and address inconsistencies across:

  • Console and UI experiences
  • Technical documentation
  • Marketing and product messaging

By participating in early design discussions and reviewing UX workflows, terminology, and error messaging, I help ensure customers receive a coherent and trustworthy experience—regardless of where they encounter the product.

docs.title: Supporting and Scaling the Technical Writing Community
docs.text:
My project leadership also extends to supporting fellow technical writers. I contribute by:

  • Mentoring writers at different career stages
  • Explaining tools, workflows, and review processes
  • Creating templates, standards, and training materials

These efforts reduce onboarding time, improve consistency, and enable teams to scale documentation efficiently while maintaining a high bar for quality.

docs.title: Tools, Practices, and Delivery
docs.text:
I organize and deliver work using a combination of Agile practices and modern documentation tooling, including:

  • Agile planning and tracking tools (Jira, Asana, Monday.com)
  • Structured authoring and content reuse with DITA
  • Continuous feedback from customers and stakeholders

By combining Agile project management, technical expertise, and customer advocacy, I consistently deliver documentation initiatives that are on time, high quality, and aligned with both product strategy and customer needs.

docs.title: Responsible AI solutions
docs.text:
Understanding how to use AI responsibly in technical writing is essential. AI can be a powerful assistant, but it cannot replace human writers. Instead, it should be used to reduce repetitive work and create space for higher-value tasks.

In this case, I explored which parts of the documentation workflow could be automated so I could focus more on writing conceptual content and creating high-quality CLI, JSON, and AWS CloudFormation examples.

These solutions were created for Amazon ECS, but are generic for other AWS services.

docs.title: Connecting documentation with the code
docs.text:
Amazon ECS uses identity-based policies as one of its core security mechanisms. It also provides a set of managed policies that grant specific permissions for customers.

To document these policies, I used the Amazon Q CLI with MCP servers to read permissions directly from the submitted code and automatically generate documentation. This approach provided several benefits:

  • Ensured the documentation stayed synchronized with the source code
  • Reduced manual effort and the risk of errors
  • Streamlined updates when permissions changed

Live Documentation: AmazonECSInstanceRolePolicyForManagedInstances

docs.title: Figma to tasks
docs.text:
Figma mock-ups are often used as starting points. For documentation, the mock-ups map to tasks that provide instructions for a job.

To document these tasks, I used the Amazon Q CLI with MCP servers to read the mock-ups from Figma, and then create a task following a defined DITA pattern. This approach provided several benefits:

  • Ensured the documentation stayed synchronized with the mock-ups
  • Reduced manual effort and the risk of errors
  • Streamlined updates when strings changed

Live Documentation: Creating an Amazon ECS blue/green deployment

docs.title: Amazon ECS API Reference
docs.text: This reference provides an overview of the Amazon ECS API operations, including request structure, required parameters, response format, and common error conditions. You use this guide when you integrate Amazon ECS operations into your automation, tooling and deployment workflows. One important aspect of this guide is to have clear and working examples.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) API enables programmatic control of containerized workloads. This includes creating and managing clusters, services, tasks, and related infrastructure components.

This reference outlines:

  • Required and optional request parameters
  • Example request and response structures
  • Authentication and IAM considerations
  • Common error messages and troubleshooting guidance

Documentation structure:

  • Pages for each API operation and data type
  • Guide is structured to display available actions for each resource
  • Request syntax with validated JSON structures
  • Constraints including what parameters must be used together in certain scenarios
  • Defaults
  • Errors users might encounter with guidance

Why this is important:

  • Prevents user trial and error
  • Reduces calls to support
  • Presents use case examples

Live Documentation: Service Deployment Actions – Amazon ECS API Reference

docs.title: Amazon ECS Developer Guide Overview
docs.text:
The Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) Developer Guide provides comprehensive guidance on how to architect, configure, and deploy applications on Amazon ECS. It covers the full range of ECS tooling—including the web console, AWS CLI, and AWS CloudFormation—and explains how ECS uses JSON-based resources such as task definitions.

Because ECS integrates with several other AWS services, the guide also introduces key concepts from Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon ECR, and foundational Docker principles that help users build and operate containerized workloads effectively.

docs.title: My Approach
docs.text:
My approach to developing this guide was highly hands-on:

  • I wrote conceptual content and created fully functional examples that customers can copy directly from the AWS documentation site.
  • I built and tested these examples in real environments to ensure accuracy and usability.
  • I participated in bug bashes and tested new ECS features

Documentation structure:

This guide has been organized using the following DITA page types:

  • Concepts
  • Tasks
  • Reference
  • Troubleshooting
